title: Free Energy Principle (FEP)
content_html:
Free Energy Principle (FEP)

The Free Energy Principle (FEP) states that any self-organising system that persists in a changing world (e.g., a living organism or an agent) must, on average, keep its sensory states within a limited, unsurprising set. In formal terms, such systems minimise an information-theoretic bound—variational free energy—on sensory surprise under a probabilistic generative model of the world. Perception, learning, action, and memory are therefore different ways the system updates beliefs, parameters, and policies to keep surprise low over time.

  • Generative model: You posit hidden causes z that generate observations x via p(x,z)=p(x|z)p(z).
  • Posterior beliefs: Because p(z|x) is often intractable, you keep a tractable approximation q(z).
  • Variational free energy: F[q] = E_q[ln q(z) - ln p(x,z)] = DKL(q(z)||p(z|x)) - ln p(x).
  • Key property: F[q] ≥ -ln p(x) (surprise). Minimising F with respect to q gives the best-possible posterior within your family; minimising F with respect to model parameters improves model evidence.
  • Equivalent view: F = E_q[-ln p(x|z)] + DKL(q(z)||p(z)) = (prediction error) + (complexity). You trade accuracy against simplicity.

From variational inference to the brain

In cortical message-passing (“predictive coding”), descending predictions are compared with ascending sensory signals; only mismatches (“prediction errors”), weighted by their precision (inverse uncertainty), update beliefs. Learning tunes the model’s parameters and precisions across timescales; memory, in this view, is the set of parameters, precisions, and cached trajectories that support prediction and planning.

Markov blankets & non-equilibrium steady-states (NESS)

FEP connects to statistical physics by assuming agents occupy a NESS: their states fluctuate within bounds rather than dissipate. A Markov blanket (sensory and active states) separates internal from external states, defining what the agent can sense and influence. Under mild assumptions, internal states come to encode a probability density over external states—hence “the brain as an inference machine.”

Expected Free Energy (EFE) & action

To choose actions, active inference evaluates policies by their expected free energy G, which admits useful decompositions:

  • Risk/ambiguity: minimise expected deviation from preferred outcomes (risk) and reduce uncertainty in outcome mappings (ambiguity).
  • Extrinsic/epistemic value: pursue preferences while seeking information (expected information gain).

Thus, the same objective explains both exploitation (goal fulfilment) and exploration (curiosity/information-seeking).

What FEP is (and is not)

  • Is: A principle (like least action) that constrains viable models of persistent, self-organising systems; specific theories (e.g., cortical microcircuits) are testable instantiations under this principle.
  • Not: A claim that organisms literally minimise thermodynamic free energy; here “free energy” is variational (ELBO), though thermodynamic links can be drawn.

Common criticisms & clarifications

  • “Unfalsifiable / too general”. Debate continues over scope, especially around Markov blankets. Responses emphasise that FEP constrains models; hypotheses are tested at the level of active-inference implementations.
  • “Exploration doesn’t follow from free-energy minimisation.” Clarifications show how EFE decomposes into information gain and preference terms—and where alternative objectives (e.g., FEEF) can be more appropriate.
  • “Thermodynamics vs variational free energy.” Modern summaries (“made simpler”) delineate the information-geometric (variational) story and its links to physics.

Memory

  • Parameters & priors (semantic structure) are the system’s long-term memory; updating them = learning.
  • Precision (uncertainty) controls what gets learned—your Select.
  • Generative replay (cached trajectories/predictive maps) supports planning and construction: Reconstruct.
